title: BEGIN, COMMIT and Transaction Boundaries
learningObjectives: Start an explicit SQLite transaction with BEGIN.
Explain the difference between explicit transactions and SQLite autocommit mode.
Choose a safe boundary for a multi-statement business operation.
Recognize why transactions should be short and always completed.

understand.concept: BEGIN starts an explicit transaction in SQLite. COMMIT ends it and makes its changes permanent. Keeping the transaction boundary around the smallest complete business operation reduces the risk of leaving a transaction open.
understand.whyItMatters: Explicit boundaries let an application decide which statements must succeed together and exactly when changes become visible as committed work.
understand.analogy: A transaction is like a sealed work packet: its related steps are accepted together or returned for correction.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL locking, isolation levels, storage durability or engine-specific transaction implementation.

explain.narrative:
## Basic transaction flow
Use BEGIN to start a transaction, execute related statements, and use COMMIT after all required work succeeds. If a statement fails, handle the error and roll back rather than committing a partial operation.

## SQLite syntax
SQLite supports BEGIN [DEFERRED | IMMEDIATE | EXCLUSIVE], COMMIT and END. A transaction started with BEGIN remains active until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

## Transaction boundaries
Keep transactions short. Do not wait for user input or make network requests while holding a write transaction. Use application error handling to guarantee that every successful BEGIN is paired with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

## Autocommit
SQLite normally runs in autocommit mode when no explicit transaction is active. A standalone statement is committed automatically when it finishes successfully.

examples.title: Update and commit order status
examples.code: BEGIN; UPDATE tx12_orders SET order_status = 'paid' WHERE order_id = 1; COMMIT; SELECT order_status FROM tx12_orders WHERE order_id = 1;

practise.guidedTask: Create an order, commit it, and retrieve the committed row. Then update its status in a second transaction.
practise.independentTask: Design a three-step inventory receiving operation. Put the related statements inside one transaction and explain when the application should commit.
hints: Statements after BEGIN belong to that transaction until it ends.
A standalone statement outside an explicit transaction is normally committed automatically.
Keep the transaction short and avoid waiting on external services inside it.

questions.prompt: Which statement begins an explicit SQLite transaction?
What ends a successful transaction and commits its changes?
questions.explanation: COMMIT makes the transaction's changes permanent.

options: The normal mode where each standalone statement is committed when it completes
A mode that commits only once per year
A command to export a database
questions.answer: The normal mode where each standalone statement is committed when it completes
questions.explanation: When no explicit transaction is active, SQLite normally commits each statement automatically.

questions.prompt: Why should transactions be kept short?
options: To reduce the time locks or transactional resources are held
questions.answer: To reduce the time locks or transactional resources are held
questions.explanation: Short transactions reduce contention and resource holding time.

questions.prompt: What should application code do if a required statement fails before COMMIT?
options: Roll back the transaction and handle the error
Close the database file without handling the transaction
questions.answer: Roll back the transaction and handle the error
questions.explanation: Rollback prevents incomplete work from being committed.
